terms.definition: Google's library for deep learning: fast arithmetic on big grids of numbers (tensors), on CPUs, GPUs and TPUs, with automatic gradients.
the part of TensorFlow for building and training networks with ready-made layers, losses and a training loop (imports start with tf.keras).
TensorFlow's array: a single number, a list, a table or a stack of tables, all of one data type.
the set of functions and classes a library offers you to call ("application programming interface").
TensorFlow's library for loading data and feeding it to a model in batches (Chapter 13).
a model made of layers of small calculating units (neurons); each layer's outputs are the next layer's inputs.
one step of a network: a group of neurons that read the same inputs; in Keras an object such as Dense(30).
one calculating unit of a layer: it multiplies each input by a weight, adds them up with a bias, and applies an activation function.
a number the network learns, one per connection between two neurons; training changes the weights.
one extra learned number per neuron, added to its weighted sum.
the small function a neuron applies to its weighted sum before passing it on, such as ReLU ("negative becomes 0"); in this chapter also: what a layer outputs is called its activation.
the activation max(0, z): positive values pass unchanged, negative values become 0.
the number training tries to make small: how wrong the model's predictions are (for example the mean squared error).
for every parameter, how much the loss would change if that parameter moved a little, and in which direction; the optimizer steps against it.
the object that turns gradients into parameter updates. SGD, RMSProp and Nadam are different update rules (Chapter 11 compares them); "nadam" in compile() picks one.
the repeated cycle: take a batch, predict, compute the loss, compute gradients, update the weights. Keras's fit() runs it for you.
a number the model learns in training: its weights and biases. (Chapter 2 used the word the same way for Scikit-Learn models.)
sending inputs through the layers to get predictions (no learning yet).
automatic differentiation: TensorFlow records the operations of the forward pass and works out every gradient exactly from that record.
TensorFlow's recorder (tf.GradientTape): operations run inside its with-block are written down, so tape.gradient() can compute gradients afterwards.
one TensorFlow operation, such as add or matrix multiply.

the code that runs one op on one kind of device (a CPU kernel, a GPU kernel). Careful: Keras also calls a layer's weight matrix its kernel, and Chapter 2's kernel was a similarity function — three uses of one word.
the computer's ordinary processor.
graphics processor: a chip with thousands of small cores, very fast at the arithmetic networks need.
tensor processing unit: Google's chip built only for deep-learning arithmetic.
a description of a calculation as a network of ops (nodes) connected by the tensors flowing between them (edges), which TensorFlow can optimize before running.
a compiler that turns code into a faster form while the program is running, not ahead of time; XLA is TensorFlow's.
TensorFlow's web page for watching training runs (loss curves and more).
a site of pretrained models you can download and reuse.
already trained by someone else, ready to reuse.
TensorFlow Extended: Google's libraries for running models in production (data checks, serving predictions with TF Serving).
the version of TensorFlow that runs models on phones and small devices; TensorFlow.js runs them in a web browser.
TensorFlow's collection of ready-made network designs, some already trained.
a rule applied to a layer's weights after each training step, e.g. "no weight may be negative".
one op inside a computation graph.
removing parts of a graph whose results nothing uses.
cannot be changed after it is created; an operation gives you a new one instead (mutable: can be changed in place).
TensorFlow's changeable tensor: its values are updated in place with assign(); a model's weights are Variables.
a number stored in 32 bits (float64: 64 bits, more exact, twice the memory). TensorFlow's default is float32, NumPy's is float64.
convert values from one data type to another, e.g. float64 to float32.
a table of numbers in rows and columns; @ multiplies two matrices.
swap rows and columns of a matrix.
NumPy's array type.
special tensors: sparse = only the non-zero values are stored; ragged = rows of different lengths; string = text. (Appendix C.)
a number that measures how well the model does, for you to read (accuracy, mean absolute error ...); unlike the loss, training does not follow it.
a small group of rows processed together in one training step (Keras default: 32).
how many digits a number keeps: 32-bit precision keeps about 7 digits, 64-bit about 16.
mean squared error: square each error and average them. A big error counts a lot (10 wrong costs 100).
a loss that squares small errors (like MSE) and grows only in a straight line for large ones (like MAE), so outliers pull less.
training converges when the loss stops going down because the parameters have settled.
one sample's error: true value minus prediction.
the real answer from the data (y_true).
has a slope everywhere, so gradients can be computed through it.
a number per training row saying how much that row counts in the loss (class weights: one per class).
turn a live object into a storable description (deserialize: rebuild the object from that description).
a function built inside another function that remembers the outer function's values (here the threshold).
a function whose job is to build and return another function, like create_huber(2.0).
the load_model() argument that maps each saved name to the real Python function or class.
a new class built on an existing one: it gets all the parent's behaviour and changes only what it redefines.
the method that returns a dictionary of an object's settings, so Keras can save it and rebuild it later.
calls the parent class's version of a method, e.g. super().__init__(**kwargs) runs the parent's setup first.
**kwargs collects any extra named arguments (name=..., reduction=...) so they can be passed on to the parent class.
how many per-sample values are combined into one number: sum them, average them, or keep them all.
a Python table of key: value pairs, like {"threshold": 2.0}.
a line starting with @ above a function; it wraps the function to change how it behaves (e.g. @tf.function).
the function that picks a layer's random starting weights.
a rule for how spread out the random starting weights are: variance 2 / (number of inputs + number of outputs).
a function that computes a penalty from a layer's weights; the penalty is added to the loss to keep the weights small.
a layer in which every neuron reads every input (tf.keras.layers.Dense). Dense(30) = 30 neurons.
L1: the sum of the absolute values of the weights (times a factor), added to the loss; L2 uses their squares instead.
an extra amount added to the loss, growing with the weights, so large weights cost something.
a single number (a tensor with no dimensions).
of all the rows the model called positive, the share that really were positive: 4 right out of 5 = 80%.
a metric that keeps running totals (counts, sums) across batches and divides only at the end, so the result is exact for the whole epoch.
one full pass over the training data.
a positive prediction that was right (false positive: a positive prediction that was wrong).
sorting rows into two classes (positive or negative).
sets a metric's running totals back to 0 (Keras 3 name; the book writes reset_states).
creates a tracked variable inside a layer or metric, so Keras saves it, resets it and (for layers) trains it.
a layer made from a plain function (tf.keras.layers.Lambda), for layers with no weights.
the layer method Keras calls once, the first time data arrives, so the layer can create weights of the right shape.
the method holding a layer's or model's forward pass: the calculation done on every input.
the size of a tensor along each direction: [None, 5] = any number of rows (None) of 5 columns.
a variable gradient descent is allowed to change; non-trainable variables (e.g. running statistics) are kept but not trained.
stretching a smaller tensor to match a bigger one in arithmetic, e.g. adding one bias vector to every row of a matrix.
a layer or model Keras must run line by line in Python instead of turning it into a graph.
a small stack of layers whose output is added back to its own input (input + layers(input)).
the path that carries a block's input past its layers so it can be added back at the end.
the if and for statements of a program: branching and repeating.
Keras's way of wiring layers by calling them on each other's outputs; it builds a fixed graph, so it cannot loop.
saving (or loading) only the numbers of a model's weights, not its design.
Keras's simplest model: a plain list of layers, each feeding the next.
called inside a layer or model's call(): adds an extra value to the loss that training minimises.
the book's call for showing an extra value during training without training on it; removed in Keras 3 (a metric object kept on the model does the same job).
a network trained to rebuild its own input from a smaller inner representation (Chapter 17).
what a layer's outputs capture about the input: the numbers it hands on.
the network's attempt to rebuild its own input from an inner layer.
estimating a slope by nudging one input by a tiny amount and seeing how much the output moved.
how much the output changes when ONE input changes a little, the others held still; the gradient is the list of them.
the autodiff method TensorFlow uses: one forward pass, then one backward pass gives the gradient for every parameter at once.
tf.stop_gradient(x): passes x forward unchanged but blocks gradients from flowing back through it.
the @tf.custom_gradient decorator: you write the derivative yourself, e.g. to avoid an overflow.
a number too big for its storage becomes inf (infinity); inf / inf gives NaN.
"not a number": the result of an impossible calculation such as inf / inf. Once it appears, it spreads.
tf.GradientTape(persistent=True): a tape that is not erased after its first gradient() call.
a layer that switches off random neurons at each training step (only while training), to fight overfitting.
a layer that standardizes its inputs using the current batch while training, and stored averages when predicting.
the optimizer method that updates the variables: it takes (gradient, variable) pairs.
adds up a list of tensors of the same shape.
turns a Python function into a TensorFlow graph that runs faster and can be exported.
the part of tf.function that reads your function's source and rewrites Python for-loops and ifs into TensorFlow ops.
the one-time run of your function with placeholder tensors, during which TensorFlow records the graph.
a tensor with a data type and a shape but no values, used while tracing.
TensorFlow's normal mode: each line runs immediately, like ordinary Python (the opposite of graph mode).
the activation log(1 + e^z): a smooth version of ReLU — always above 0, close to 0 for very negative z and close to z for large z.
rescaling each example's own features to average 0 and spread 1 (then a learned scale and offset), row by row, so it works the same on one example as on many.
an image set of 70,000 small grey photos of clothes, 28 x 28 pixels, in 10 classes such as T-shirt, trouser and ankle boot (60,000 for training, 10,000 for testing).
